The Pacific sierra (Scomberomorus sierra) attains a maximum recorded fork length of 99 centimeters [Li = 99 centimeters], a value consistent with the upper size range documented for medium-bodied scombrids in the eastern Pacific. Field surveys along the coasts of Mexico and Central America indicate that individuals grow rapidly during their first year, with most fish exceeding 40 centimeters by the end of their first growing season. This species exhibits a relatively compressed life history compared to larger tuna species, with the oldest documented individuals reaching approximately 1,825 days [am = approximately 1,825 days] in waters maintained at 25.8 °C [T = 25.8 °C], based on otolith increment analysis conducted on specimens from the Gulf of California. The longevity estimate of roughly five years places the Pacific sierra among the shorter-lived members of its genus, a trait that likely reflects the energetic demands of its fast predatory lifestyle in warm, productive coastal waters.

Reproductive development in the Pacific sierra proceeds rapidly under the warm thermal regime typical of its tropical and subtropical habitat. When water temperatures average 25.8 °C [T = 25.8 °C], puberty, defined by the onset of active gametogenesis, is attained at approximately 730 days [tp = approximately 730 days]. Histological examination of gonadal tissue from populations off the Pacific coast of Mexico shows that vitellogenesis commences during the second year of life, with the first spawning event typically occurring shortly thereafter. The total length at which 50 percent of individuals reach puberty has been estimated at 59.3 centimeters [Lp = 59.3 centimeters], a size that corresponds well with the observed age at maturity. This length-based threshold appears to be relatively consistent across the species range, although slight variations have been noted between inshore and offshore populations.

Under the thermal conditions of the spawning season, at an average water temperature of 25.8 °C [T = 25.8 °C], the gonadosomatic index (GSI) of reproductively active female Pacific sierra peaks at 30% [GSI = 30%]. This value reflects the substantial allocation of somatic resources toward ovarian development during the reproductive period. Spawning is thought to occur in multiple batches over an extended season, as is common among tropical scombrids, with gravid individuals captured from late spring through early autumn. Ovarian biopsies indicate that oocyte development is asynchronous, allowing for continuous recruitment of vitellogenic oocytes throughout the spawning window.

Neonatal life begins with the emergence of yolk-sac larvae following eclosion, a stage during which the developing fish relies entirely on endogenous yolk reserves — a pattern common to many teleost species. The wet weight at birth, estimated from the diameter of the fertilized ovum, is approximately 0.000065 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000065 grams], a remarkably small initial mass that places this species among those with the smallest hatchlings relative to adult body size within the family Scombridae. The yolk-sac larva remains lecithotrophic for a brief period, typically lasting only two to three days before the mouth opens and first exogenous feeding commences. During this endotrophic phase, rapid absorption of yolk nutrients fuels early organogenesis, including the differentiation of the retina and the development of the jaw apparatus necessary for capturing planktonic prey.

Comparative life-history analysis across the genus Scomberomorus reveals that the Pacific sierra occupies an intermediate position in terms of both growth rate and longevity. While the maximum reported fork length of 99 centimeters [Li = 99 centimeters] is modest relative to the giant Scomberomorus cavalla, it exceeds the typical adult size of the smaller Scomberomorus regalis. At 730 days [tp = 730 days], individuals reach sexual maturity, and the total lifespan extends to 1,825 days [am = 1,825 days] under stable thermal conditions at 25.8 °C [T = 25.8 °C], generating a life-history trajectory that prioritizes early reproductive output over extended somatic growth. This strategy is well suited to the variable nearshore environments the species inhabits, where high natural mortality rates among juveniles may select for rapid attainment of sexual maturity. The total length at maturity of 59.3 centimeters [Lp = 59.3 centimeters] further reinforces the pattern of early investment in reproduction, a common feature among medium-sized scombrids occupying productive coastal upwelling zones.
